questions.sub_topic: Apparent depth through two plane liquid layers
questions.image_alt: Coin beneath two horizontal layers viewed from air: upper layer depth 6 cm, refractive index 3/2; lower layer depth 4 cm, refractive index 4/3. Interfaces are plane and parallel.
questions.question: A coin lies at the bottom of the two transparent, immiscible liquid layers shown. It is viewed from air close to the normal. Neglect container thickness. What is its apparent depth below the top liquid surface, and would reversing the order of the layers (keeping each layer's depth) change this apparent depth?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(7\ \mathrm{cm}\); unchanged.
Given: \(t_1=6\ \mathrm{cm},\ n_1=\tfrac32;\quad t_2=4\ \mathrm{cm},\ n_2=\tfrac43;\quad n_{\text{air}}=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(d_{\text{app}}=\displaystyle\sum_i\frac{t_i}{n_i}\quad(\text{near-normal viewing})\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{t_1}{n_1}=\dfrac{6}{3/2}=4\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{t_2}{n_2}=\dfrac{4}{4/3}=3\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Worked derivation: \[d_{\text{app}}=4+3=7\ \mathrm{cm}\]
Check: \[\text{reversed order}:\ \frac{4}{4/3}+\frac{6}{3/2}=3+4=7\ \mathrm{cm}\]
Why: \(\dfrac{t_1}{n_1}+\dfrac{t_2}{n_2}=\dfrac{t_2}{n_2}+\dfrac{t_1}{n_1}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(6+4=10\ \mathrm{cm}\) (\(n_i=1\)); (B) \(7\ \mathrm{cm}\) but \(3+4=4+3\); (D) \(6\cdot\tfrac32+4\cdot\tfrac43=\tfrac{43}{3}\ \mathrm{cm}\) (\(t_in_i\)).
Key point: \(d_{\text{app}}=\displaystyle\sum_i\frac{t_i}{n_i}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Series RLC phasors and real power
questions.question: A series circuit contains an ideal resistor, inductor and capacitor driven by a sinusoidal source. The rms current is 2 A, and the rms voltage magnitudes across R, L and C are 8 V, 10 V and 4 V, respectively. What are the source rms voltage and average power supplied?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(10\ \mathrm V\) and \(16\ \mathrm W\).
Given: \(I=2\ \mathrm A,\quad V_R=8\ \mathrm V,\quad V_L=10\ \mathrm V,\quad V_C=4\ \mathrm V\ (\text{rms})\)
Formula/Principle: \(V=\sqrt{V_R^2+(V_L-V_C)^2},\quad P=IV_R=VI\cos\phi\)
Step 1: \(V_L-V_C=10-4=6\ \mathrm V\)
Step 2: \(V=\sqrt{8^2+6^2}=\sqrt{100}=10\ \mathrm V\)
Worked derivation: \[P=IV_R=2\times8=16\ \mathrm W\]
Check: \[\cos\phi=\frac{V_R}{V}=0.8,\quad VI\cos\phi=10\times2\times0.8=16\ \mathrm W;\qquad R=\frac82=4\ \Omega,\ I^2R=16\ \mathrm W\]
Why: \(V_L\ \text{leads }I\text{ by }90^\circ,\quad V_C\ \text{lags }I\text{ by }90^\circ,\quad\langle P_L\rangle=\langle P_C\rangle=0\)
Why not the others: (B) \(8+10+4=22\ \mathrm V,\ 22\times2=44\ \mathrm W\) (scalar sum); (C) \(VI=10\times2=20\ \mathrm{VA}\) (\(\cos\phi\) omitted); (D) \(8+10-4=14\ \mathrm V,\ 14\times2=28\ \mathrm W\).
Key point: \(P=VI\cos\phi=I^2R\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.sub_topic: Half-wave rectification and mean power in a resistor
questions.question: An ideal diode and a resistor R form a half-wave rectifier driven by \(v(t)=V_0\sin\omega t\). There is no smoothing capacitor. What is the ratio of average power dissipated in R to the average power that the same sinusoidal source would dissipate in R if R were connected directly to it? Neglect source resistance and diode voltage drop.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(1/2\).
Given: \(v(t)=V_0\sin\omega t,\quad T=\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega},\quad\text{ideal diode}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\langle P\rangle=\dfrac{1}{T}\displaystyle\int_0^T\frac{v_R^2}{R}\,dt\)
Step 1: \(P_{\text{direct}}=\dfrac{V_0^2}{RT}\displaystyle\int_0^T\sin^2\omega t\,dt=\dfrac{V_0^2}{RT}\cdot\dfrac T2=\dfrac{V_0^2}{2R}\)
Step 2: \(v_R=V_0\sin\omega t\ \left(0<t<\tfrac T2\right),\quad v_R=0\ \left(\tfrac T2<t<T\right)\)
Step 3: \(P_{\text{half}}=\dfrac{V_0^2}{RT}\displaystyle\int_0^{T/2}\sin^2\omega t\,dt=\dfrac{V_0^2}{RT}\cdot\dfrac T4=\dfrac{V_0^2}{4R}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{P_{\text{half}}}{P_{\text{direct}}}=\frac{V_0^2/4R}{V_0^2/2R}=\frac12\]
Check: \[V_{\text{rms,half}}=\frac{V_0}{2},\quad V_{\text{rms,direct}}=\frac{V_0}{\sqrt2},\quad\left(\frac{V_0/2}{V_0/\sqrt2}\right)^2=\frac12\]
Why: \(\langle P\rangle=\dfrac{\langle v_R^2\rangle}{R}\neq\dfrac{\langle v_R\rangle^2}{R}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{V_0/2}{V_0/\sqrt2}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\) (rms voltages, not powers); (C) \(\dfrac{(V_0/2)^2}{V_0^2}=\dfrac14\) (\(V_0\) for \(V_{\text{rms,direct}}\)); (D) \(v_R=0\ \text{for }\tfrac T2<t<T\).
Key point: \(P\propto V_{\text{rms}}^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Two-colour interference, phase reversal and minimum slab thickness
questions.question: An ideal interferometer uses light of vacuum wavelengths 600 nm and 1000 nm. For each colour the two interfering beams are coherent and have equal amplitudes. At a reference point the geometric optical paths are initially equal, but one beam has an additional phase of \(\pi\) for each colour, so both colours are dark there. A plane glass slab is inserted normally in one path, replacing an equal thickness of air without otherwise changing the geometry. Its refractive index is 1.50 for both colours. What is the smallest positive slab thickness that makes the reference point an interference maximum for both colours?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(3.0\,\mu\mathrm m\).
Given: \(\lambda_1=600\ \mathrm{nm},\quad\lambda_2=1000\ \mathrm{nm},\quad n=1.50,\quad\phi_0=\pi\)
Formula/Principle: \(\delta=(n-1)t,\quad\phi=\pi+\dfrac{2\pi\delta}{\lambda}=2\pi k\)
Step 1: \(\delta=\left(k-\tfrac12\right)\lambda\Rightarrow\delta=(2r+1)\dfrac{\lambda_1}{2}=(2s+1)\dfrac{\lambda_2}{2}\)
Step 2: \((2r+1)(300\ \mathrm{nm})=(2s+1)(500\ \mathrm{nm})\Rightarrow3(2r+1)=5(2s+1)\)
Step 3: \(2r+1=5,\quad2s+1=3\Rightarrow\delta=1500\ \mathrm{nm}\)
Worked derivation: \[t=\frac{\delta}{n-1}=\frac{1500\ \mathrm{nm}}{0.50}=3000\ \mathrm{nm}=3.0\ \mu\mathrm m\]
Check: \[\frac{1500}{600}=2.5,\qquad\frac{1500}{1000}=1.5\]
Why: \(\text{bright}\iff\dfrac{\delta}{\lambda}=k-\tfrac12\ \text{for both }\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\delta=300\ \mathrm{nm}:\ \dfrac{300}{1000}=0.3\); (B) \(\delta=600\ \mathrm{nm}:\ \dfrac{600}{600}=1.0,\ \dfrac{600}{1000}=0.6\); (C) \(\delta=900\ \mathrm{nm}:\ \dfrac{900}{600}=1.5,\ \dfrac{900}{1000}=0.9\).
Key point: \(\delta=(n-1)t=\operatorname{lcm}_{\text{odd}}\left(\tfrac{\lambda_1}{2},\tfrac{\lambda_2}{2}\right)\)
